name: Culinary — The Working Kitchen

stations.why: The bench case: the line as a first-period cook meets it, before any one hazard is taken apart on its own.
The board anchored, the edge honed, and the claw grip that keeps a prep cook's own knuckles between the blade and the cut — plus the mandoline nobody runs bare-handed.
The deli slicer taken apart for a changeover the way a machine shop would: the cord locked out before the guard comes off, and the interlock proven before power goes back in.
The 60-quart floor mixer whose guard interlock gets proven, not assumed, before anything goes in the bowl — and whose scrape-down only ever happens on a machine that's actually stopped.
The vat only gets opened once it has actually cooled — cold and wheeled beats hot and carried, every single change.
The system over the line only works if the filters, the links and the pull path are checked before the day a flare-up actually tests them.
A gas smell is a procedure, not a guess — no spark searches for it, and the valve, not the nose, decides when the line is clear.
Cold storage as its own procedure: the inside release proven before the door is trusted, 41 °F confirmed, and stock put away raw-below-ready in the order the Food Code sets.
The delivery that stocks that cooler in the first place: every cold, frozen and hot item probed at the dock and refused outside the Food Code's own limits, before anything reaches a shelf.
The other half of the clock: a cooked batch brought down through 70 °F in two hours and 41 °F in six, with the reheat-or-discard call for the one that misses it.
The dish machine and the three-compartment sink: chemical lines checked, the sanitiser strip-tested and logged, and an eyewash proven clear before the first jug is opened.
Servicing the under-sink grease interceptor: the confined-space question answered correctly, the 25 percent rule read off the stick, and the waste sealed for the hauler rather than sent down a drain.
An allergen order on the line: the ticket called back, the purple board and dedicated pan pulled, and the plate walked to the pass by the cook who built it.
The banquet line: hot boxes probed before they're loaded, chafers lit lid-open, the buffet walked before doors, and a pull-down cooled or discarded to the rule.
The school lunch line under the National School Lunch Program: the meal pattern's five components, offer versus serve, the wells probed and the count reconciled for the reimbursement claim.
The grill and sauté station's own hazard, worked as a drill: handles in, a dry pan, a flambé cleared of the filters, and cool water run the full twenty minutes.

summary: One kitchen, station by station, from the receiving dock to the dish pit. The hazards are the ones a cook actually meets — heat, blades, chemicals, cold, gas and the clock — and the standard behind every step is the one an inspector or a union steward would cite.
union: UNITE HERE Local 2 cooks, dishwashers and banquet staff; AFSCME and SEIU school and hospital food service
